explanations.answer: To love and serve Him with all your heart
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD asks Israel to fear Him by walking in all His ways, to love Him, and to serve Him “…with all your heart and with all your soul…” Notice he doesn't say "serve Him when it's convenient." I've stamped cookies with a tired mustache before, and showing up and meaning it are two different batches.

explanations.answer: To build Him a house made of cedar
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't put a cedar house on this list. He asks Israel to fear the LORD by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve Him with all their heart and soul, and to keep His commandments and statutes. Not one plank is mentioned. Friend, I'm glad, because I'd hate to see what a cedar bill looks like.

explanations.answer: To bring Him a lamb each morning
explanations.explanation: A lamb each morning isn't on Moses' list here, baker. What he names is fearing the LORD by walking in all His ways, loving Him, and serving Him with all the heart and soul. He adds keeping the LORD's commandments and statutes. That's a list about the whole heart, not a morning errand. Good thing, too, because I can barely get the ovens preheated before my second yawn.

That's it, baker. Moses says the commandments and statutes are given "…for your own good?" So he's not handing Israel a pile of rules to trip over. Think of a recipe card: the steps feel like a lot until the cookies come out right.

Not quite, friend. Moses doesn't call the commandments a punishment. He says the LORD is giving them "…for your own good?" I know a rule can feel like a burnt batch, but that isn't how Moses describes it.

Close to something you might expect, but that isn't the word here. Moses says the commandments and statutes are given for Israel's own good. Testing isn't mentioned in this verse. Think of the timer on my oven: it's there to help the batch, not to catch anybody.

Right, baker. Moses says the LORD set His affection on Israel's fathers and loved them, and that He has chosen their descendants “…above all the peoples, even to this day.” Here's the part I love: the heavens and the earth are His, so He had every choice there was. And He still set His affection on them.

Moses says the opposite, friend. He says the LORD set His affection on Israel's fathers and loved them, and that He has chosen their descendants “…above all the peoples, even to this day.” So the answer here is true. Just before it, Moses says the heavens and the earth belong to the LORD, so He had the whole world to choose from.

Yes, friend. Moses says, "Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more." I think he's pointing at something deeper than the outside. When the preacher says hearts, you know he isn't talking about your hat.

Good guess, but Moses doesn't say sons here. The word is hearts: "Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more." He's talking to all Israel about what's inside. The verse never mentions the next generation at all.

Households is a sneaky one, baker, but that's not the word. Moses says, "Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more." The hearts are the target here. Your house can stay the way it is, dishes and all.

Not this time, baker. Moses says the opposite: the LORD "…executes justice for the fatherless and widow…" He doesn't leave them to fend for themselves. Right after saying He accepts no bribe, Moses shows who the LORD stands up for.

That's right, friend. Moses says the LORD “…executes justice for the fatherless and widow…” Leaving them to fend for themselves isn't what he describes. He says it right after telling Israel the LORD shows no partiality and accepts no bribe.

Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD “…loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing.” That love shows up as real provision, not just a nice feeling. Then Moses turns it around: Israel must love the foreigner too, since they themselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

Moses says it plainly, friend: the LORD "…loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing." So the answer here is true. And that matters, because the very next verse asks Israel to love the foreigner too.

That's it, baker. Moses says, “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.” That's the reason he gives them. I think anyone who's been the new person in a room knows what he's getting at.

Moses never says anything about foreigners fighting alongside Israel. His reason is that they themselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. That's the whole reason he gives. It's about their own past, friend, not a future favor.

No harvest-sharing here, baker. Moses gives one reason: Israel was once foreigners in the land of Egypt. He isn't talking about what they'll get back. Love for the foreigner comes from remembering where they stood.

Not quite, friend. Moses says their fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD has made Israel “…as numerous as the stars in the sky.” So Israel isn't that small today. Seventy is where they started, and the stars are the comparison Moses picks.

Right, baker. Moses says the fathers went down to Egypt seventy in all, and now the LORD has made Israel "…as numerous as the stars in the sky." From a small group to a sky full. I know a little something about stars, and I'm still counting on them to show up.

Yes, baker. Moses says the LORD "…made the waters of the Red Sea engulf them as they pursued you…" The Egyptian army, horses and chariots included, was chasing Israel when it happened. Moses wants them to remember it because their own eyes saw it.
Not here, friend. In this verse Moses says the LORD made the waters of the Red Sea engulf the Egyptian army, horses and chariots. Darkness isn't what he names. It's the waters.

Sand doesn't make an appearance, baker. Moses says the LORD made the waters of the Red Sea engulf the Egyptian army as they pursued Israel. The waters are the answer. Sand is better kept for the beach.

That's right, baker. Moses says it happened in the midst of all the Israelites, when "…the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them…" Dathan and Abiram were sons of Eliab the Reubenite. Moses says it to remind everyone what they saw with their own eyes.

Fire does show up in that story, friend, but not for these two. It consumed the 250 men who were offering incense (Numbers 16:35). For Dathan and Abiram, Moses says the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them. It's an easy mix-up since the events sit so close.
Moses doesn't mention a plague here, baker. He says the earth opened its mouth and swallowed Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab the Reubenite. This is a heavy part.

Moses says more than that, friend. The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram, “…their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them.” So the households and tents went too. I think this one hurts.

That's right, baker. Moses says the earth opened its mouth and swallowed Dathan and Abiram, “…their households, their tents, and every living thing that belonged to them.” So it wasn't just the two men. Their households and tents went with them.

Yes, baker. Moses says keeping every commandment is “…so that you may have the strength to go in and possess the land…” Israel is about to cross the Jordan, and strength is the word he gives for going in. I've tried hauling a full cookie rack on pure confidence, and confidence doesn't lift a thing.

Wealth isn't the word, friend. Moses says keeping every commandment is so that Israel may have the strength to go in and possess the land. They're about to cross the Jordan. Strength is what he names.

No weapons in this verse, baker. Moses says keeping every commandment is so that Israel may have the strength to go in and possess the land. Nothing about swords or spears. Even a mustache like mine would take the strength option.

explanations.answer: It drinks the rain from heaven
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Moses says the land across the Jordan is "…a land of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven." That's the contrast with Egypt, where they irrigated on foot. Here the water comes down from above.

explanations.answer: A great river floods it yearly
explanations.explanation: A flooding river isn't what Moses names, friend. He says the land is one of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven. The water comes from above. That's the whole picture he paints.

Wells don't appear in this verse, baker. Moses says the land drinks in the rain from heaven. It's a land of mountains and valleys, and that's different from Egypt, where they irrigated on foot (Deuteronomy 11:10).

Not quite, friend. Moses says the eyes of the LORD your God are always on the land, "…from the beginning to the end of the year." That's the whole year, not just harvest. He's watching over it the entire time.
Right, baker. Moses says it's a land for which the LORD cares, and His eyes are always on it "…from the beginning to the end of the year." So it isn't only harvest time. Every day of the year counts.

Yes, baker. The promise is, “…I will provide grass in the fields for your livestock…” and Moses adds that they will eat and be satisfied. So both the animals and the people are fed. A full table is a good sign.

Water from a rock isn't in this promise, friend. For the livestock, the promise says, “…I will provide grass in the fields for your livestock…” It comes right after the promise of rain in season. The grass is the answer.

Shelter isn't what's promised here, baker. For the livestock, the promise says, “…I will provide grass in the fields for your livestock…” and Moses adds that you will eat and be satisfied. Valleys do come up earlier, where the land drinks in the rain from heaven (Deuteronomy 11:11), but not for the animals. A nice roof over an empty field would be a sad review from any cow.

Yes, baker. Moses says if Israel turns aside to other gods, "He will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain…" Then the land won't yield its produce, and they will soon perish from the good land. It's a serious warning, and he says it straight.
Shake isn't the word, friend. Moses says the LORD “…will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain…” It comes with the warning that the land won't yield its produce. This is a heavy part.
Darken isn't the word, baker. Moses says the LORD "…will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain…" Without rain, the land won't yield its produce. The word to remember is shut.

explanations.answer: Morning and night at home and away
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Moses says to speak about them “…when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” That covers at home and away, and from waking to bedtime. It isn't a once-a-week thing, it's a way of living.

explanations.answer: Only on feast days at the altar
explanations.explanation: Moses says something much bigger, friend. He wants the words spoken about “…when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” No altar or feast day is named in that verse. Those are everyday moments at home and on the road.

explanations.answer: Once a year at the Passover
explanations.explanation: Once a year wouldn't match what Moses says, baker. He says to speak about these words “…when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” That's sitting, walking, lying down and getting up, not one date on the calendar. Repeat a recipe that often and you'd never forget it.
Yes, baker. Moses says, "Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates…" So the words are right where you come and go. It's hard to miss a message when you walk past it twice a day.
Moses says it outright, friend: "Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates…" So the answer is true. Every trip in and out would put the words in front of them.

That's right, baker. Moses says if they keep these commands, "…the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you." Greater and stronger than Israel, and still the LORD drives them out. The size of the other side isn't the deciding thing.

Moses says just the opposite, friend. He says that if Israel keeps these commands, "…the LORD will drive out all these nations before you, and you will dispossess nations greater and stronger than you." So the answer is true. It's the LORD doing the driving out.

Moses says something bigger than that, friend. He says, "No man will be able to stand against you…" That's no one at all, not even a few strong men. It also says the LORD will put fear and dread of them upon all the land.
That's right, baker. Moses says, "No man will be able to stand against you…" Not a few, not any. The LORD will put the fear and dread of Israel on all the land, as He has promised.

Yes, baker. The word is curse. Moses sets two outcomes in front of Israel: a blessing for obeying the LORD's commandments, and a curse for disobeying them. The curse is tied to turning aside and following other gods they have not known. He doesn't blur it, and he doesn't leave them guessing which road leads where.

Plague isn't the word, friend. Moses sets a blessing next to a curse, and the curse is for those who disobey and turn aside to other gods. It's a heavy choice, and he says it plainly. The word he uses is curse.
Battle isn't what Moses names, baker. He sets a blessing for obeying against a curse for disobeying and following other gods. Those are the two things in front of Israel. The word is curse.

That's it, baker. Gerizim is the mountain for the blessing, and Ebal is the one for the curse. Moses even adds directions: across the Jordan, west of the road toward the sunset, near the Oak of Moreh. Directions with a landmark tree in them are my kind of map, though I'd still manage to get lost.

Carmel doesn't show up in this passage, friend. Moses names two mountains for the proclaiming: the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Keep Gerizim for the blessing and Ebal for the curse, and you've got the pair.

Sinai is a big name, baker, but Moses isn't pointing there. He says the blessing goes on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. Those mountains are across the Jordan, in the land Israel is about to enter. Gerizim is the answer.
